title: Steamed Fish with Ginger and Spring Onion
subtitle: Cantonese steamed white fish with hot soy and aromatics
excerpt: Steaming fish with ginger and spring onion is one of the most elegant techniques in Cantonese cooking. The fish stays tender and moist; the final pour of smoking-hot oil over the aromatics releases a dramatic sizzle. It is fast, light, and delicious.
sourceNotes: Steaming whole fish or fillets with ginger, spring onion, and soy sauce is one of the most classic preparations in Cantonese cuisine. The technique preserves the delicate texture of the fish and the final pour of hot oil over the aromatics releases a fragrant sizzle that is central to the dish.

content.text: Timing is everything with steamed fish. The fish can go from perfectly cooked to dry in two minutes. Have everything ready before the fish goes into the steamer -- the spring onion and ginger julienned, the soy measured, and the oil in a small pan ready to heat. Once the fish is done, the rest takes under a minute.

items.prepNote: or any firm white fish -- skin on if possible
peeled and cut into fine matchsticks
heated until smoking -- for the final pour

content.text: Score the fish fillets with two or three diagonal cuts on each side. Rub with a little salt inside the cuts.
Set up a steamer over a wok or large saucepan of boiling water. Place the fish on a heatproof plate that fits inside.
Scatter half the ginger over the fish. Steam for 8 to 10 minutes, depending on thickness. The fish is done when it flakes easily at the thickest part.
Drain away any liquid from the plate. Lay the spring onion strips and remaining ginger on top of the fish.
Heat the oil in a small pan over high heat until smoking. Pour it directly over the spring onion and ginger -- it will sizzle dramatically.
Drizzle the soy sauce over the top. Serve immediately with steamed rice.

items.fix: For fillets, 8 minutes is usually enough. Check at 7 minutes -- the fish should be opaque and flake with a fork. A whole fish of 600g needs about 10 minutes. Do not leave it in the steamer after cooking.

content.text: Steamed fish is the test of a Cantonese cook. The technique is simple but the timing must be precise. The final pour of hot oil is the dramatic moment -- it wilts the spring onion and ginger in an instant. This dish is served at family dinners and banquets alike.
